items.title: [bbc.co.uk] African negotiators press for triple adaptation funding at COP31
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

African negotiators at the U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, are seeking to triple annual adaptation finance to $120 billion by 2035, using an annual baseline of $40 billion they say developed countries committed to provide by 2025. The proposal was not accepted for formal negotiations, and the European Union says the priority should be delivering existing pledges and making funds easier to access. Twenty-three African countries, including Uganda and Malawi, have yet to submit national adaptation plans that can help identify climate risks and support funding requests. The U.N. estimates developing countries will need $300 billion a year by 2035, but they received about 10% of that amount from developed countries in 2024. African civil society groups are also pressing for finance that does not add to debt and for measurable commitments on fossil fuel reductions. COP31 was scheduled to close on Friday, Nov. 20, with 21 issues unresolved.

items.title: [bbc.com] Brazil activates protective measures after about 20 isolated Awá approach
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

About 20 Indigenous Awá living in isolation approached the Guajajara village of Tawari on Monday, November 16, in Arariboia Indigenous Territory, in the Brazilian state of Maranhão; they received yams and returned to the forest. Members of the Guajajara community recorded the encounter, and the organization Survival International shared the footage. The National Foundation for Indigenous Peoples (Funai) and Indigenous health personnel are in the area. The government activated an emergency coordination mechanism to assess the situation and health risks. Authorities said they are still assessing the initial information and that this isolated approach does not mean the Awá have abandoned their isolation. The reason for the visit has not been confirmed; Survival International linked it to pressure from illegal loggers, hunters, and ranchers on the territory. Local residents voiced concern about the thinness of some children and older people. There is also concern about the risk of infections, given the group’s limited exposure to common pathogens.

items.title: [news.un.org] COP31 ministers face deadlock over fossil fuels, finance and science
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Ministers at the United Nations COP31 climate summit in Antalya remained deadlocked Wednesday over a final agreement, with 21 issues unresolved and only days left before the conference’s scheduled close Friday, Nov. 20. Disputes include whether to call for a transition away from fossil fuels, how to fund climate adaptation and whether to set a global electrification goal. A draft political deal released Monday included competing proposals on fossil fuels, climate finance, the 1.5°C goal, science and trade. Turkey’s proposal to raise electricity’s share of global final energy use to 35% by 2035 has support from 75 countries, but some governments oppose including it in the final text. Countries also disagree over when the next assessments from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the UN-backed climate science body, should be ready. Vulnerable countries want them before the 2028 global review, while others favor 2029. Ministers met informally Wednesday to seek compromises; a revised draft was expected Thursday.

At a late Friday plenary, delegates approved technical decisions but left the main political text unresolved. COP31 President Murat Kurum said a new draft was expected Saturday.

Investigators have linked the communications overload behind Friday’s nationwide U.S. flight halt to a recently installed router at a Federal Aviation Administration radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, according to a Wall Street Journal investigation. A radar installation in Amarillo, Texas, also generated abnormal traffic. The disruption affected 17 of the FAA’s 22 en-route centers after initial communication glitches appeared at its Indianapolis center. Officials are examining whether the fault involved defective equipment, installation or configuration. They said the system stabilized after the Arkansas and Texas devices were disconnected and a router-broadcast feature was disabled across the FAA’s roughly 60 Juniper routers. Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper Networks, said its devices operated as intended. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said investigators had not determined the cause. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford predicted that airlines would largely restore schedules by late Sunday, Nov. 15; more than 530 Sunday flights had already been canceled by Saturday evening.

items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Lightning struck NASA’s Apollo 12 Saturn V rocket twice within seconds of its Nov. 14, 1969, launch, disrupting spacecraft telemetry and endangering the mission. Mission Control engineer John Aaron recognized the readings from an earlier test and recommended switching the Signal Conditioning Equipment to its auxiliary setting, which restored the data. Investigators concluded the rocket and its conductive exhaust plume had triggered a discharge in an electrically charged part of the atmosphere, even though no active thunderstorm lay along the immediate flight path. NASA expanded launch weather restrictions to account for atmospheric electrical conditions, not only visible lightning and thunderstorms.

items.title: [energylivenews.com] IEA warns Hormuz crisis will permanently reshape global energy priorities
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The International Energy Agency’s 2026 World Energy Outlook says the Iran war and disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have caused a historic shock to energy supplies, with lasting effects on how countries secure power and fuel. IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said he sees no credible route back to the pre-crisis energy system. The agency says the shock is strengthening the case for electrification and domestic energy sources, including renewables and nuclear power, but also encouraging some countries to retain coal as backup. Under current and proposed policies, electricity is projected to supply 29% of final energy use by 2035, below the 35% goal set at the COP31 climate summit. Oil demand is expected to level off around 2030; coal demand is projected to fall 14% from 2025 to 2035, while planned liquefied natural gas (LNG) export capacity could exceed demand by 70 billion cubic meters in 2035. The outlook also warns that demand growth will strain power networks: the world needs at least 25 million kilometers of new power lines over the next decade and upgrades or replacements for another 15 million kilometers. Major grid projects can take five to 15 years to plan, permit and complete. The IEA says its scenarios are possible pathways, not forecasts.

items.title: [phys.org] Cosmology researchers test rival accounts of dark energy and cosmic expansion
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Researchers have proposed two different explanations for dark energy, the component estimated to make up about 70% of the universe’s energy. A team from the University of British Columbia and the University of Sheffield says quantum chromodynamics (QCD)—the established theory of the strong nuclear force—could account for the observed acceleration of cosmic expansion through properties of the quantum vacuum, without requiring a new particle or field. The team found that its model fit observations of supernovae and early-universe radiation about as well as standard cosmological models. Separately, a University of Ottawa study tested a model called CCC+TL, which attributes effects usually assigned to dark matter and dark energy to changing physical constants and “tired light.” The researchers say it matched several observations, including light-element abundances and cosmic-chronometer measurements. The model also estimates the universe is 26.7 billion years old. Both proposals remain theoretical, and the QCD team plans to test its calculations against future space-telescope data.

items.content_html:

British Columbia’s Civil Resolution Tribunal has overturned a $100,000 penalty against social media platform X for failing to delete an intimate image posted without a woman’s consent, ruling that blocking access to it in Canada was a reasonable step under provincial law. The tribunal said the law did not make X liable after it blocked Canadian access to the image, which remained available outside Canada. The decision reversed a September 2025 penalty for failing to comply with an order to delete it. The tribunal accepted X’s argument that requiring worldwide removal could interfere with other countries’ legal systems and cited a 2024 Australian case as persuasive but not binding. Outgoing B.C. Attorney General Niki Sharma criticized X’s refusal to remove the image and said governments may need to strengthen laws or pursue legal action. The tribunal also rejected X’s request to require the complainant to pay more than US$100,000 in legal fees.

Private fusion investment remains concentrated in the United States and China. European Union companies had attracted €712 million of about €13 billion tracked worldwide by November 2025.

items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Germany’s governing coalition has approved a one-year electricity-tax cut for 2027, reducing the levy for households to the European Union minimum at an estimated cost of about €5 billion. The government plans to fund the cut through lower renewable-energy subsidy costs, expecting high wholesale prices to boost wind and solar revenues. If power prices fall, subsidy costs could rise, leaving a funding shortfall. Germany’s Economy Ministry said it still expected prices to remain elevated next year; the coalition has said it would prepare a further package if savings prove insufficient. The measure still needs to be included in the 2027 budget, which parliament is expected to vote on next week.

items.title: [english.aawsat.com] Iraqi forces enter Iran-backed militia stronghold, establish joint command

Iraqi government forces entered Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday in the first federal deployment there in 12 years and opened a joint security headquarters under an arrangement with Kataib Hezbollah, the Iran-backed armed group that has controlled the area. Baghdad says the deployment will reorganize security and protect oil infrastructure after an investigation alleged oil smuggling; Kataib Hezbollah denies the accusations. The new command, led by Federal Police and involving army, police, Popular Mobilization Forces and Energy Police units, will coordinate security across the district. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi called on troops to show restraint and said the operation aimed to bring armed groups under state authority without fighting. Whether Kataib Hezbollah is withdrawing remains disputed: the group denied leaving, while Iraqi security sources said three of its brigades had departed and officials described a phased transfer that could take a month. Officials also announced that the main road through the area would reopen to civilian traffic on Saturday, Nov. 21. Displaced residents’ return depends on security checks, repairs and the restoration of services.

items.title: [abcnews.com] Trump replaces national cyber director after outages disrupt US services
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

President Donald Trump replaced National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross with Pentagon Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies as acting director after a week of outages disrupted aviation, banking, communications and government systems. The incidents have drawn scrutiny of the administration’s response, although officials say there is no evidence of a coordinated cyberattack or a connection among the failures. A source familiar with the White House’s thinking said Trump supported Cairncross’s removal because he lacked strong cybersecurity credentials. Trump said Friday, “I didn’t think that person was good enough”. Axios reported that Chief of Staff Stephen Miller pushed for the change on similar grounds. Cairncross, a former Republican National Committee executive, said he was proud of his work in the role. Davies has held cybersecurity and technology leadership jobs at Unilever, Estée Lauder, Barclays-Africa Group, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Siemens. Davies will serve temporarily. A permanent director must be nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate, which Democrats are due to control in January. Cybersecurity experts say companies’ rapid efforts to patch software vulnerabilities may be behind some disruptions, as advanced AI tools make those flaws easier to find.
